claims.text: Selective outward diffusion of Al, and secondarily Cr, governs protective-scale persistence in CrFeCoNiAl above 900 °C.
Selective oxidation forms an external Al2O3 scale and an inner Cr2O3 layer.
The duplex oxide remains adherent when oxidation kinetics are moderate.
Excessive Al depletion triggers substantial subsurface phase transformations that cause oxide cracking or spallation.
The studied material is a nominally equiatomic AlCrCoFeNi alloy.
The as-cast alloy consists of approximately 79% BCC and 21% ordered B2 phases.
The initial alloy has a maze-like, spinodally decomposed microstructure.
Heating produces intermediate FCC and Cr-Fe-rich sigma phases from the initial BCC/B2 substrate.
Oxide growth produces an Al-depleted subsurface zone.
Higher oxygen availability accelerates oxidation, increases scale thickness, and promotes Al consumption.
A controlled external Al-rich and inner Cr-rich duplex scale protects the substrate.
Rapid oxidation weakens scale adherence through Al-depletion-induced subsurface phase transformations.
Atmospheric-air exposure will produce a thicker duplex Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale than vacuum exposure.
Atmospheric-air exposure will produce pronounced subsurface Al depletion and associated phase transformations.
Vacuum exposure will produce a much thinner oxide layer composed predominantly of Al2O3.
The polished as-cast room-temperature baseline has BCC/B2 phases and no thermally grown oxide scale.
The proposed heating cycle reaches 1100 °C at 10 °C/min in 50 °C increments with a 5-minute hold at each setpoint.
The vacuum comparison is specified at approximately 4.2×10^-6 atm total pressure and an oxygen partial pressure of approximately 8.82×10^-7 atm.
The proposed mechanism is relevant to similar CrFeCoNiAl alloys in oxidative or corrosive high-temperature environments.
